assumptions.statement: Households will regularly keep their fridge and pantry inventory up to date with acceptable effort.
assumptions.rationale: PantryPal's primary differentiation relies on knowing existing household inventory. However, in-target participants explicitly reject high-effort data entry: dual-income couple P02 stated, "Setup has to be fast. If I need to type in my whole pantry I'll quit on day two." (1 of 5 in-target households), and working family P03 noted, "I think the biggest thing is not making it feel like homework." (1 of 5 in-target households). Adjacent segments (irregular couple P05, flatmates P10) expressed identical drop-off risks. If inventory logging causes friction, users abandon the app immediately.

assumptions.statement: A rigid weekly dinner plan and weekly shopping list format fits the daily planning rhythms of target cooking households.
assumptions.rationale: Weekly planning fits structured weekly shoppers like working families P01, P03, and P04 (3 of 5 in-target households). However, daily and spontaneous shoppers abandon advance calendars: adjacent irregular couple P05 noted, "Planning ahead stresses me out. A plan I don't follow feels like failure, so I decide on the day." and "I tried a meal-planning app once. By Thursday I hadn't followed the plan and I just stopped opening it." (1 of 2 adjacent households). Daily shoppers shop "almost every day and buy as I go" (P05:t5; in-target retired couple P09:t5, 1 of 5 in-target households). In-target users also demand full control: "I want to edit the plan easily. I don't want an app dictating to me." (P01:t8, P02:t8).

assumptions.statement: Target households are willing to pay a recurring monthly subscription (EUR 3.50 to EUR 6.99/month) for an inventory-based meal planner.
assumptions.rationale: Competitor subscriptions range from EUR 2.99/month (C:PlanPlate) to EUR 6.99/month (C:MealLoop), with market median stated willingness to pay at EUR 3.50 per month (S05). In-target working family P01 stated, "A few euros a month, maybe, if it clearly saves me money on groceries." (supported by P04:t9, and adjacent flatmate P10:t9). However, dual-income couple P02 anchored strictly against free utilities: "Maybe five or six euros. More than that and I'd just keep my notes app." (P02:t9, 1 of 5 in-target households). Others demand free versions entirely: working family P03 ("A free version with ads would also be fine.", 1 of 5 in-target households), adjacent couple P05 ("Honestly I wouldn't pay for it. I'd want a free version."), and retired couple P09 ("Honestly I wouldn't pay for it. I'd want a free version.", 1 of 5 in-target households). Overall adoption of meal-planning apps remains low at 11% (S03).

assumptions.statement: All households of two or more people cooking at home on weeknights suffer from acute dinner planning friction and food waste.
assumptions.rationale: While food waste (19% discarded, S01; EUR 118 weekly grocery spend, S02) and decision time (22 minutes, S04) affect families P01, P03, P04 and couple P02 (4 of 5 in-target households), being in the demographic target does not guarantee having the problem. Retired couple P09 (1 of 5 in-target households) cooks nightly but reports zero friction: "We cook every day, we've done it for forty years. I know what we like and what is in the cupboard. Our daughter says we should use an app for the shopping list, but we have never needed one." (P09:t1) and "Not much, honestly. Sometimes I'd like fresh ideas, but it isn't a problem." (P09:t2). The target customer definition must be constrained to households lacking settled cooking routines.

assumptions.statement: Computer vision or automated scanning can reliably capture loose fridge perishables and pantry contents without continuous manual corrections.
assumptions.rationale: Competitors use photos for recipe generation (C:FridgeChef) or barcodes for pantry expiry tracking (C:PantryGenie). However, common household waste consists of partial, unpackaged fresh produce such as "Half a cucumber, wilted herbs, yoghurt that expired last week." (P02:t2) and a "bag of spinach" (P01:t4). Tracking partial quantities and variable freshness via camera or barcode without manual tuning is technologically difficult and risks feeling like homework (P03:t10).

assumptions.statement: Interpersonal mealtime arguments are a primary customer pain point driving adoption among multi-person households.
assumptions.rationale: The idea brief claims the app helps households stop arguing about what is for dinner. However, arguing was reported by only 1 in-target household: dual-income couple P02 ("argued for ten minutes about what to eat and ended up ordering pizza", P02:t3, 1 of 5 in-target households). In contrast, the concrete shared friction across 2 of 5 in-target households (P02, P04) and adjacent flatmates (P10) is uncoordinated shopping and duplicate buying: "My partner and I both shop, and we constantly end up with two packs of the same thing" (P02:t2) and "My wife bought chicken and I bought chicken, the same afternoon. We ended up with six breasts and a freezer that was already full." (P04:t4).

experiments.hypothesis: Households will maintain an inventory for 14 days if logging requires under two minutes per grocery run via low-effort input (photo or receipt capture) rather than manual text entry.
experiments.method: Recruit 20 in-target households (12 working families with children, 8 dual-income couples). Provide a concierge/wizard-of-oz prototype testing three low-effort onboarding methods: fridge photo recognition, barcode scan, and online grocery receipt forwarding. Track daily inventory updates, item decay accuracy, and logging time over two weeks.
experiments.success_metric: At least 60% of participating households update their inventory after grocery runs across 14 days with an average logging time under 2 minutes per trip. If fewer than 40% sustain tracking, pivot away from full pantry tracking to lightweight staple checklists or manual perishable-only flags.

experiments.hypothesis: Offering flexible same-day 'what can I cook tonight with what I have' suggestions achieves higher meal execution and lower abandonment than a rigid 7-day advance meal plan.
experiments.method: Run a 2-week split test with 30 cooking households (15 weekly grocery shoppers, 15 daily or irregular shoppers across in-target families/couples and adjacent flexible households). Cohort A receives a fixed weekly meal plan and shopping list generated on Sunday. Cohort B receives a 5:00 PM same-day suggestion based on current fridge contents with one-tap recipe swaps. Measure recipe completion rates and drop-off.
experiments.success_metric: Cohort B achieves >= 70% dinner plan execution among daily/irregular shoppers, compared to < 40% execution in Cohort A. If weekly plan abandonment in Cohort A exceeds 50%, pivot core navigation from a calendar planner to same-day suggestions with an optional weekly planning mode for bulk shoppers.

experiments.hypothesis: Target household cooks will commit to a paid subscription at EUR 3.50 to EUR 4.99/month when messaging demonstrates measurable grocery cost savings.
experiments.method: Launch smoke-test landing pages with targeted ads reaching 1,500 household cooks. Test three price points: EUR 3.50/month (matching S05 median anchor), EUR 4.49/month (matching C:SupperSync), and EUR 6.99/month (matching C:MealLoop), with a call-to-action button to subscribe with payment details following a 7-day trial.
experiments.success_metric: Paid click-through conversion rate >= 5% on the EUR 3.50/month tier, with at least 3% on EUR 4.49/month. If conversion drops below 2% across all paid tiers, pivot business model to freemium with ad support or supermarket affiliate integration.

experiments.hypothesis: Positioning the app around shared shopping list coordination and avoiding duplicate grocery purchases generates higher user acquisition than positioning around 'stop arguing about what's for dinner'.
experiments.method: Run an A/B landing page test targeting 1,000 multi-person household meal decision-makers. Variant A headlines: 'Stop arguing about what's for dinner'. Variant B headlines: 'Sync your household grocery list and stop buying duplicate groceries'. Track email waitlist conversions.
experiments.success_metric: Variant B achieves at least a 2x higher visitor-to-signup conversion rate than Variant A. If Variant A converts < 2%, drop the 'stop arguing' angle from product messaging in favour of shared coordination.

open_questions: What are the specific countries, income levels, and recruitment backgrounds of the target customer base?
How does meal planning and inventory tracking behaviour hold up over extended time (usage retention, feature drop-off beyond the first week)?
What is the objectively measured volume and financial cost of food waste per household, as opposed to self-estimated figures (e.g. EUR 20-30 weekly in P03:t2 or EUR 200 in P08:t2)?
How do households prefer to input what they own (fridge camera photos, barcode scanning, paper receipt scanning, or supermarket digital order history)?
What are the retention metrics, active user numbers, and churn rates for existing competitors like C:MealLoop, C:FridgeChef, and C:PantryGenie?
What is the total addressable market size specifically for multi-person households who cook weeknights and suffer meal-planning friction, considering overall app adoption is only 11% (S03)?
Who within the multi-person household decides the meal plan, who does the physical grocery shopping, and who holds purchasing authority for an app subscription?
recommendation_reason: PantryPal's foundational premise depends on households maintaining an active pantry and fridge inventory, which represents the highest usability risk: participants explicitly warn that setup must not 'feel like homework' (P03:t10) and that typing in a pantry causes users to quit on day two (P02:t8). In addition, advance weekly planning alienates daily and spontaneous shoppers (P05, P08, P09), willingness to pay is unvalidated against free alternatives like notes apps (P02:t9), and competitor analysis shows that inventory-aware apps already exist (C:FridgeChef, C:PantryGenie). The team must test low-effort inventory input mechanisms and compare weekly planning with same-day suggestions before committing capital to full software development.
